sources.title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg

discussion.body: The word carrying the most weight here is "ceasefire". Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had targeted Ukraine's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week. A truce that one side counts in dozens of violations is really a scoreboard.

It also has a commodity attached to it. Trump called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with Vladimir Putin to supply diesel — which goes some way to explaining why Ukraine resuming strikes on Russian oil facilities drew his ire.

Whatever the diplomacy is called, the air war has a rate. Russia's defence ministry said it shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday — a number that says as much about drones as mass-produced munitions as it does about air defence.

items.title: Fires at Two St Petersburg Oil Facilities After an Overnight Attack Kills at Least One
items.body: At least one person was killed and at least five injured in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that targeted two of the city's oil facilities, the region's governor, Alexander Beglov, said. He said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot, that 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged, and that Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed. Kyiv has not commented on the strikes. A logistics centre belonging to Ozon — described by the BBC as Russia's Amazon — and a data centre belonging to VKontakte were also hit.

sources.title: Living with a stink? Technology might help

discussion.body: The interesting shift is attribution. Before Des Moines installed monitors, officials drove out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air. Sensors turn "something smells" into a number with an address attached.

A number isn't a remedy, though. Milpitas has an odour problem, residents there have endured rank smells from industrial sites including a 342-acre landfill for decades, and the community's hopes are pinned on technology — which rather suggests the smell is still around to be monitored.

The fabric-conditioner line earns its keep. Fabric conditioner doesn't remove a smell; it argues with it. Calling an industrial deodoriser one is a polite way of saying the odour is still in the room, just outnumbered.

items.title: Absorb It, React With It, or Burn It: Three Ways to Fight an Industrial Smell
items.body:
Industrial odour control sorts roughly into three families: systems that absorb odours, systems that convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction, and systems that burn them away.

Experts on fixing industrial odours say the best of these technologies, used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for a smell. That kind of kit is expensive, though, and some operators choose simpler, cheaper options — masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.

Odour experts were dubious about the effectiveness of those industrial-scale air fresheners. Consultant Micheal Bull is blunter than most, likening them to fabric conditioner.

sources.title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Stuns With $15 Million Debut, ‘Street Fighter’ Leads With $31 Million

discussion.body: The audience numbers are the real surprise: around 70% of opening weekend crowds were under 35, and exit polls found 90% of ticket buyers would definitely recommend it. That is not the traditional documentary crowd, and it is why the film is expanding nationwide.

Careful with the genre lesson. Analyst David A. Gross describes a market where documentaries rarely get a wide release — roughly one every other year — averaging $3 million over their first three days. This film never entered that market; it is an outlier event, and outliers are not trends.

Scarcity did some of the work. More than 2,000 sold-out screenings means plenty of would-be ticket buyers were turned away, and their money simply arrives in week two and week three as the film widens.

items.title: "You Can See Everything" Took $15 Million From 855 Screens — About $17,500 Each
items.body:
"You Can See Everything" — Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's film about Elizabeth Holmes — took $15 million from just 855 theaters on its opening weekend, second only to "Street Fighter's" $30 million from 3,575 venues. Divide it out and that is roughly $17,500 a screen for the documentary against about $8,400 for the video-game adaptation.

A24 produced the film in secret over three years for about $7 million and reported more than 2,000 sold-out screenings. Heading into the weekend it was projected at $7 million to $8 million — a figure Variety called remarkable for a documentary, especially one that doesn't involve music or capture a wildly popular concert. It runs nearly three hours and, until two months ago, wasn't on anyone's radar.

sources.title: Why the ugly history of IQ testing matters for AI and education

discussion.body: The phrase to watch is "raw IQ". Sam Altman has been discussing artificial general intelligence that matches or surpasses human capabilities, and the same person has said children born today, including his own, will never be more intelligent than AI from a raw IQ perspective. A historian of IQ testing reads that sentence differently than a press release does.

The danger isn't a machine outscoring a child; it's the sorting. Universities claimed a major stake as measurers of intelligence, and the Rutgers AI Lab's worry is about technology shaping people to fit a narrow standard of intelligence, health, ability or social worth — evaluation systems that encode ideas about who has potential.

And the stakes were never only academic. Eugenic ideas of intelligence, the piece argues, deeply shaped residential schools and their colonial legacies — a reminder that measuring who counts is never purely a classroom matter.

items.title: Before AI Measured Students, Universities Measured "Intelligence"
items.body:
In the early 20th century, university disciplines and academic careers were built by crafting scientific-sounding definitions and measures of "intelligence" and "IQ," a scholar of the history of Canadian higher education writes in The Conversation Canada.

The example given: Peter Sandiford, head of the University of Toronto's department of educational research, tested the "intelligence" of Chinese and Japanese Canadian students in British Columbia in the 1920s.

The argument is that this history should shape how teaching and learning are positioned now. One live instance: because of the fear of AI cheating, educators are grappling with forms of assessment, and the prescription offered here is to focus, more than ever, on the collaboration and critical thinking students do — and how they connect ideas.

sources.title: Data centres: Opposing them and developing them are not the only two choices

discussion.body: The deeper problem is that these are self-referential ratios: a building graded against its own IT load, not against the watershed or the substation next door. You could fill a province with excellent PUE scores and still discover the grid is the binding constraint.

That is an argument for publication, not for scrapping the metric. A comparable, inspectable number is worth having — the trouble starts when nothing forces anyone to disclose it before approval, and nothing follows when a project drifts from its promises.

items.title: Power Usage Effectiveness Measures a Data Centre's Overhead, Not Its Value
items.body: A patient's chart in Thunder Bay, a bank card in Halifax: the request travels to a building humming with servers, storage, network equipment, backup power and cooling. The Conversation Canada's framing is deliberately unromantic — not mythical “AI factories,” not innocuous warehouses, but industrial infrastructure with real appetites for electricity, water and land. Which raises the question of what the standard numbers actually tell you. Power usage effectiveness (PUE) is a facility's total energy divided by the energy its computers use; the theoretical ideal is one, meaning every watt beyond the servers is a watt of overhead. Natural Resources Canada's best-practice guide makes the obvious point that PUE ignores the useful work the servers perform. A facility can score beautifully and still be doing very little, and efficiency is not the same as local impact. Canada's Responsible Data Centre Development Principles, unveiled on Sept. 3 by the federal government and the Federation of Canadian Municipalities with 23 industry signatories, sit on top of that gap. They are a common national baseline — and, explicitly, not binding federal law, a permit or an approval. A ratio can tell you how tightly a building runs. It cannot tell you what the building owes the grid it sits on.

sources.title: If you have the scratch, they have the scares

discussion.body: An emerging directors program is cheap optionality: you get many short-form filmmakers at low cost, and occasionally one of them arrives with an audience already built into the IP. The moths quote is charming, but the structure underneath it is a portfolio.

One enormous gross is a data point, not a validated pipeline. And the headline figure is revenue rather than profit — a $10 million budget is only the visible part of getting a film into thousands of theatres.

items.title: $10 Million In, $400 Million Out, and a Studio Pipeline Behind It
items.body: A horror feature about a liminal space that exists beyond our own reality, made for about $10 million — petty cash by Hollywood standards — grossed more than $400 million worldwide last May. It began as a short on YouTube. The film is one title from Blumhouse Atomic Monster, the newly merged studio headed by president and CEO Abhijay Prakash and by Michael Clear, president of Atomic Monster. Clear also leads the studio's emerging directors program, which is the part worth holding next to those numbers: the route from a short to a wide release is institutional plumbing, not a lucky lightning strike. Clear's own account of the appetite is less corporate than strategic — “We're drawn like moths to a flame to things that are scary.”

sources.title: Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s ‘Jengira’s Magnificent Dream,’ With Tilda Swinton, Boarded by ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Mexican Co-Producer Piano

discussion.body: It is also a ruthless production choice. Period detail is expensive and often wrong; a single handheld object does the expository work of an entire art department, and it lets the same landscape serve every century.

Elegant until it has to carry too much. A prop asked to be the only temporal marker in a film about memory and the supernatural risks reading as a gimmick — every ring or flashlight beam becomes a puzzle piece the audience is told to solve.

items.title: Apichatpong's Next Film Uses Cell Phones as the Only Sign of Which Era You're In
items.body: Apichatpong Weerasethakul's follow-up to Memory has a formal device that costs almost nothing and does a great deal: 1970s sci-fi aesthetics inside a world with no other period markers except cell phones. A phone in frame is the whole clock. In Jengira's Magnificent Dream, a Thai widow named Jengira travels to the ancient rock forest of Sigiriya in central Sri Lanka to scatter her husband's ashes, and the film blurs the boundaries between memory, history and the supernatural. Tilda Swinton, who starred in Memory, is attached. Piano — the Mexican production and distribution company behind Ruben Östlund's Palme d'Or-winning Triangle of Sadness — has boarded the project. There is something pleasing about a film that treats time as a property of objects rather than of calendars. Most movies announce their era with cars, costumes and hairstyles; this one asks you to notice a screen.

sources.title: Pope Leo says he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery

discussion.body: The window is the Vatican's oldest communication channel, and the cheers are evidence about the crowd rather than about the patient. What the appearance establishes is that he can appear — which is not nothing, and not a prognosis either.

Fair, but the risk runs the other way too: a wave and a steady voice are the kind of images that soften a hard diagnosis into a comeback story. Adenocarcinoma of the lung is the sentence to keep in the same paragraph as the applause.

items.title: A Pope Back at the Window, Four Days After Lung Surgery
items.body: Pope Leo XIV appeared at the window overlooking St Peter's Square on Sunday and told the crowd he would gradually resume his activities, describing the phase as behind him and his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed. The crowd erupted in cheers; a delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the blessing. The 71-year-old pontiff had the lobe removed on Tuesday, the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate, and the surgery confirmed adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Two facts sit close together here and do different work. A pope at a window is news about visibility, morale and the sheer theatre of convalescence in public. A confirmed adenocarcinoma is news about a disease — the most common type, in a 71-year-old, in a role with no retirement age built into its script.
